findings.headline: £45m commercial property investment holding has £4.5m unrealised loss with expiring protection
findings.detail: The council holds £45.455m in pooled property and multi-asset funds (£50m nominal value), representing an unrealised loss of £4.455m. The council has set aside a £3.911m reserve against this loss, but explicitly noted the statutory override protecting against investment losses is "highly unlikely to be extended beyond 31 March 2029", creating a 2-3 year window for potential crystallisation.
findings.matters: Crystallisation of the £4.5m loss would directly deplete reserves and require additional borrowing to offset, further reducing financial flexibility
findings.figures: Investment current fair value £45.545m (£50m nominal); unrealised loss £4.455m; reserve held £3.911m; override expires 31 March 2029
findings.quote: The current Fair Value Profit and Loss of the remaining funds is £45.545m (£50m nominal), so there was a deficit of £4.455m at 31 March 2026. As the override is highly unlikely to be extended beyond 31 March 2029 the Council has decided to maintain this reserve

findings.headline: Capital programme forecast to require £55m+ in additional borrowing over next two years
findings.detail: The liability benchmark forecasts additional borrowing of £21.3m in 2026-27 and £34.3m in 2027-28 to fund capital expenditure. The Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to grow from £703.8m in 2026 to £778.1m by 2029, indicating ongoing material increases in total debt.
findings.matters: Rising debt levels increase future revenue commitments for debt service; particularly concerning as PWLB borrowing rates have risen significantly (10-year rate 5.38% → 5.72% during the year), making new borrowing more expensive
findings.figures: Additional borrowing 2026-27: £21.272m; 2027-28: £34.257m; CFR growing from £703.759m (2026) to £778.056m (2029); 10-year PWLB rate moved from 5.38% to 5.72%
findings.quote: The long-term liability benchmark assumes an additional borrowing requirement of £21.272m in 2026-27, £34.257m in 2027-28, to fund new and existing capital expenditure

findings.headline: Council deployed reserves to cover schools funding deficit, reducing financial buffers
findings.detail: Usable reserves fell by £1.4m during the year, with the council using reserves to cover the dedicated schools grant deficit. This contributed to the net borrowing requirement rising £70.3m (25%) to £356.9m, meaning the council is now dependent on substantially higher borrowing to fund operations and capital.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or fund capital needs without additional borrowing, and may signal underlying service funding pressures
findings.figures: Usable reserves £323.574m → £322.189m; net borrowing requirement increased from £286.596m to £356.906m
findings.quote: Some of the Council's useable reserves have been used to fund the DSG deficit, therefore increasing its borrowing requirement.

findings.headline: Tibshelf New Primary School scheme with £7.013m budget remains at feasibility stage with only £0.018m expended
findings.detail: Scheme is still at feasibility stage with officers working with school and stakeholders to determine the best outcome. Only £0.018m has been spent, all incurred in 2025-26.
findings.matters: Early-stage feasibility on a £7m scheme signals risk of further programme delays or cost escalation in education capital delivery.
findings.figures: £7.013m budget, £0.018m spent to date, £6.995m underspend
findings.quote: This scheme is still at feasibility stage. Officers are working with the school and relevant stakeholders to determine the best possible outcome for the new Primary School. The only expenditure incurred to date is £0.018m on this scheme, all of which has been in 2025-26.

findings.headline: Capital receipts achieved £29.964m against forecast of £6.000m—nearly five times the expected level
findings.detail: Property Services working with Legal achieved asset disposals substantially above forecast, providing significant additional capital financing in 2025-26.
findings.matters: Signals either material improvement in asset sales capacity or significant forecasting weakness; either way is material for financial planning.
findings.figures: £6.000m forecast, £29.964m actual
findings.quote: The forecast for capital receipts for 2025-26 was £6.000m, but Property Services working closely with the Legal team were able to dispose of assets for a total of £29.964m.

findings.headline: New Capital Starts Programme will require £36.140m borrowing in 2027-28, a 3.5x increase from 2025-26 and the largest single-year debt commitment in the three-year programme
findings.detail: Three-year Capital Starts Programme of £94.456m approved with £55.973m additional borrowing. Borrowing profile is £9.528m in 2025-26, £10.305m in 2026-27, then jumps to £36.140m in 2027-28.
findings.matters: Significant future debt service commitments will increase revenue budget pressure in 2028-29 onwards and signal upcoming constraints on council spending flexibility.
findings.quote: New borrowing of £9.528m will be required in 2025-26, £10.305m in 2026-27 and £36.140m in 2027-28.

findings.headline: Two major care facilities have latent roof defects with liability disputes and potential for additional council funding beyond budget
findings.detail: Darley Dale Specialist Care Centre and Heanor Specialist Care Centre both have leaking flat roofs. Liability for repairs remains unclear, external legal advice has been sought, and the council may need to fund repairs itself if remaining budgets prove insufficient.
findings.matters: Unresolved liability on two major council assets creates operational risk, litigation exposure, and potential for cost overruns beyond current budgets.
findings.figures: Darley Dale: £10.520m budget (£0.081m underspend); Heanor: £9.750m budget (£0.782m overspend to date)
findings.quote: There are latent defects due to leaks in the flat roof. The negotiation for the work is still being finalised by Legal... alternatively the Council might need to fund the repairs which may require additional funding.

findings.headline: Waste Treatment Facility procurement concluded without contract award and council conducting urgent review of project viability
findings.detail: The facility, approved for rectification in February 2023, has completed procurement but no contract has been awarded. Council is now undertaking a rapid review of future options for the project, with a report to Cabinet expected later in the year.
findings.matters: A major capital commitment (£95m+) originally intended to be operational is stalled at procurement stage with uncertain path forward, signalling potential project restructure or cancellation.
findings.figures: £95.930m budget in 2025-26, £94.172m spent to date
findings.quote: no contract has been awarded as this time. The Council is carrying out a rapid review of future options for the project, and a report will be presented to Cabinet later in the year to recommend a way forward.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council operating under significant financial and capacity pressures; Internal Audit held vacant posts following leavers
findings.detail: The Council has continued to operate under significant financial and capacity pressures. Internal Audit has had to hold vacant posts following leavers, manage secondments and long-term sickness absence. These pressures were actively managed but reflect broader organisational strain.
findings.matters: Capacity constraints in the internal control and assurance functions directly impact the council's ability to identify and remediate control weaknesses. Limited audit capacity may mean material risks go undetected.
findings.figures: Held vacant posts; managed secondment and long-term sickness absence
findings.quote: The Council has continued to operate under significant financial and capacity pressures, requiring a disciplined and risk-focused approach to the management of Internal Audit resources. Since August 2023, the emphasis has been on maintaining assurance and ensuring that limited resources are deployed effectively. During the year this included holding vacant posts following leavers, a secondment and managing the impact of long-term sickness absence.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Only 23% of audit recommendations implemented on original timeline; 43% on revised dates
findings.detail: KPI 6.1 shows only 23% of audit recommendations were implemented by their original target dates (target 75%), while KPI 6.2 shows 43% of recommendations with revised dates were met (target 90%). The report notes this 'weakens assurance and increases the risk that known control weaknesses persist longer than necessary.'
findings.matters: Poor recommendation implementation discipline means control weaknesses identified by audit remain unaddressed. This extends exposure to identified risks and suggests weak accountability for completing remedial actions.
findings.figures: KPI 6.1: 23% on original timeline (target 75%); KPI 6.2: 43% on revised dates (target 90%)
findings.quote: implementation has frequently been delayed, with agreed deadlines often revised or met after the original target date. This practice weakens assurance and increases the risk that known control weaknesses persist longer than necessary.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Management responses to audit reports seldom meet 15-day target; only 34% compliant year-end
findings.detail: KPI 5.1 shows management compliance with the 15 working day target for providing agreed responses to draft audit reports fell to 34% year-end (target 90%), with an average response time of 28 working days. This pattern held throughout the year (33-55% compliance).
findings.matters: Slow management responses to audit findings delay remedial action and indicate either capacity constraints or lack of urgency in addressing control weaknesses. This slows the control improvement cycle.
findings.figures: 34% compliance year-end; target 90%; average response time 28 working days
findings.quote: the target of providing agreed responses within 15 working days was seldom met, indicating capacity pressures or lack of urgency in some cases

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Governance Action Tracker shows high number of outstanding actions, some unresolved for several years
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement Action Tracker continued to show a high number of outstanding actions at end of Q4, with a number of these actions remaining unresolved for several years. This undermines the principle of continuous improvement and effective governance, and echoes concerns raised by External Audit.
findings.matters: Multi-year unresolved governance actions indicate weak accountability and follow-through. External Audit has also raised concerns about accuracy and completeness of governance reporting, suggesting control environment is weaker than disclosed.
findings.figures: High number of outstanding actions; several unresolved for years
findings.quote: This was reflected in the Annual Governance Statement (AGS) Action Tracker, which continued to show a high number of outstanding actions at the end of Quarter 4. A number of these actions have remained unresolved for several years, undermining the principles of continuous improvement and effective governance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Digital Services Risk Register was critical gap, not fully developed until late Q3 of 2025/26
findings.detail: The absence of a comprehensive Digital Services Risk Register represented a critical gap. While progress was eventually made, registers were not fully developed or refreshed until late Quarter 3, and due to senior leadership changes in Digital Services, were not fully scrutinised by the Audit Committee, limiting assurance over a strategically significant risk area.
findings.matters: Digital services are critical infrastructure for modern councils. A critical gap in risk management coverage and delayed development of core risk registers suggests weak oversight capacity and operational governance during a period of digital transformation.
findings.figures: Gap remained until late Q3 2025/26; not fully scrutinised by Audit Committee
findings.quote: A significant and longstanding concern related to digital risk management. As noted in the previous Annual Report, the absence of a comprehensive Digital Services Risk Register represented a critical gap. While progress was made, registers were not fully developed or refreshed until late Quarter 3 of 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Children's Services showing ongoing and significant overspends driven by demand and placement costs
findings.detail: The council is experiencing continued significant overspends within Children's Services, driven by demand pressures and placement costs. This is described as a continuation of issues from previous years, indicating a persistent problem without resolution.
findings.matters: Children's Services demand-driven overspends are symptomatic of underlying cost control issues and demographic/legislative pressures that will not self-correct. Lenders assess whether a council can absorb such pressures from existing reserves or will require additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Overspends described as 'ongoing and significant'; continuation from previous years
findings.quote: Ongoing and significant overspends, particularly within Children's Services driven by demand pressures and placement costs, represent a continuation of issues seen in previous years

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: No Assurance opinion issued for AI governance; AI governance framework judged inadequate
findings.detail: AI governance received a No Assurance opinion, indicating control has been judged inadequate due to systems weaknesses, gaps and non-compliance in numerous key areas. This is listed alongside recurring Limited Assurance findings in Agency Spend and other high-risk areas.
findings.matters: No Assurance rating means the system is open to significant risk of error, loss, misappropriation or abuse and requires immediate remedial action. As councils increasingly use AI, this governance gap represents material operational and reputational risk.
findings.figures: No Assurance rating; also Limited Assurance in Agency Spend (recurring)
findings.quote: In particular, Limited and No Assurance opinions remain concentrated in areas of elevated operational and strategic risk, including a No Assurance opinion in respect of Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Limited assurance opinion issued for the third consecutive year
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive concluded a Limited assurance opinion, unchanged from the previous two years. This reflects that while improvements have been made in some areas, significant weaknesses remain concentrated in higher-risk areas and pace of improvement has not been sufficient.
findings.matters: Three consecutive years of Limited assurance indicates persistent systemic control weaknesses that expose council objectives to higher risk of failure. A lender needs to know that the council's internal control environment is not substantially improving despite acknowledged management awareness.
findings.figures: Third consecutive year; Limited Assurance means significant weaknesses and non-compliance have been identified which expose system objectives to high risk of failure
findings.quote: This Annual Internal Audit Opinion reflects the third consecutive year in which a Limited level of assurance has been concluded.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee Member Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Digital and information governance identified as key risk area requiring strengthened control arrangements
findings.detail: The improvement plan prioritises strengthened arrangements in key risk areas including digital and information governance, alongside enhanced oversight of governance and risk and improved timeliness of audit actions.
findings.matters: Identified weaknesses in digital and information governance expose the council to data breach, cyber incident, and information control failures with financial and operational consequences.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: strengthened arrangements in key risk areas including digital and information governance, to support sustainable improvement in assurance over time

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee Member Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council struggles to deliver agreed audit improvements on time and with accountability
findings.detail: The audit report identifies that the council's key challenge is no longer awareness of control issues, but ensuring timely and consistent delivery of agreed corrective actions alongside strengthened ownership and accountability across services.
findings.matters: Slow implementation of audit recommendations indicates control improvements are stalling, suggesting previously identified weaknesses remain unresolved and new risks may be accumulating.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The key challenge is no longer awareness of issues, but ensuring timely and consistent delivery of agreed actions, alongside strengthened ownership and accountability across services.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee Member Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal audit opinion for 2025-26 remains Limited due to significant control issues in higher-risk areas
findings.detail: The annual audit opinion on the council's governance, risk management and control framework is Limited, reflecting continued presence of significant control issues in higher-risk areas and inconsistent pace of improvement implementation. While there is evidence of progress including improved audit coverage and reduction in Limited/No Assurance audit outcomes, improvements are not yet sufficiently embedded.
findings.matters: A Limited audit opinion indicates governance and control weaknesses that directly affect the reliability of the council's financial control environment and reporting.
findings.figures: Limited opinion (unchanged from prior year implied); reduction in Limited/No Assurance outcomes reported but not quantified
findings.quote: For 2025/26, the overall opinion remains Limited, reflecting the continued presence of significant control issues in higher-risk areas and the inconsistent pace at which agreed improvements are being implemented.

findings.paper_title: Performance Monitoring and Budget Monitoring Outturn 2025-26 as at Quarter 4 (31 March 2026)
findings.headline: £5m budgeted for Local Government Reorganisation preparation in 2026-27, with more funding likely needed
findings.detail: The council is using Flexible Capital Receipts to fund LGR preparation, with £5m initially allocated for 2026-27 and a note that 'Updates will be provided to Cabinet on the costs incurred for LGR over the coming months and whether more funding is required'. LGR is proposed to achieve efficiency, accountability and value, but the cost envelope is uncertain.
findings.matters: A major structural reorganization carries execution risk and cost overrun risk; the council acknowledges that the £5m may prove insufficient, creating a contingent cost pressure.
findings.figures: Flexible Capital Receipts for LGR preparation £5.000m (2026-27); total FCR available for projects £25.195m; other LGR-related costs (staff termination on failed care home transfer) £3.300m
findings.quote: Approval is also sought to use £5.000m of FCR to meet the costs of Local Government Reorganisation preparation. This is an initial provision for costs that will be incurred to prepare for LGR at the County Council. Updates will be provided to Cabinet on the costs incurred for LGR over the coming months and whether more funding is required.

findings.paper_title: Performance Monitoring and Budget Monitoring Outturn 2025-26 as at Quarter 4 (31 March 2026)
findings.headline: General Reserve strengthened to £37m but DSG deficit is held separately, creating a £9.3m hidden liability
findings.detail: The General Reserve increased to £37.035m (from £39.566m opening balance after year-end drawdowns), representing 4.8% of revenue budget and above the £35m minimum policy. However, the £93.3m DSG deficit is held as a separate reserve liability. After Phase 1 government support covers 90% of the DSG deficit, the council faces a £9.331m unfunded liability that will crystallize by 2028 unless Phase 2/2028-29 arrangements are more generous.
findings.matters: While headline reserves look adequate, the ring-fenced £9.3m DSG liability reduces true discretionary reserve headroom; it represents a 25% downside risk to reserve strength if government support falls short.
findings.figures: General Reserve £37.035m; minimum policy £35m; reserve as % of budget 4.8%; cumulative DSG deficit £93.308m; unfunded DSG liability £9.331m
findings.quote: Following the favourable outturn in 2024-25 the Council changed its reserves policy in Feb 2026 to set a requirement to have a minimum General Reserve of £35m.

findings.paper_title: Performance Monitoring and Budget Monitoring Outturn 2025-26 as at Quarter 4 (31 March 2026)
findings.headline: £8.1m of red-rated savings not delivered in-year; overall savings delivery at 93.8% of target
findings.detail: The council set a savings target of £37.5m but achieved only £35.2m (93.8%), with £8.1m of red-rated savings not delivered. These were replaced with other savings elsewhere. This miss indicates the council's efficiency programme is not tracking as planned and carries delivery risk.
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls of 6% signal that the council's transformation programme is slipping; if this trend continues into 2026-27 and beyond, the council faces further budget pressure.
findings.figures: Savings target £37.499m; actual delivery £35.172m; red-rated savings not delivered £8.103m; delivery rate 93.8%
findings.quote: The 2025-26 Revenue Budget includes savings targets totalling £37.499m. Savings totalling £35.172m were achieved in year (93.8% of the target). The Red rated savings of £8.103m were not delivered in year but were replaced with other savings

findings.paper_title: Performance Monitoring and Budget Monitoring Outturn 2025-26 as at Quarter 4 (31 March 2026)
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £8.8m includes £4.8m bad debt provision and £4.7m pressure on residential placements
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £8.8m (2.6% of budget), materially higher than Q3 forecast of £6.5m. The year-end bad debt provision of £4.799m was charged to the service. Underlying pressures include £4.7m on residential and nursing care (market pressures plus double-running costs), £1.4m on Supported Living, and a £3.9m shortfall in delivering the Community Charge (non-residential care) income target.
findings.matters: The large bad debt charge signals collection difficulty; combined with market-driven placement costs and an £3.9m income shortfall, this indicates the service cost pressures are worsening rather than stabilizing.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care overspend £8.818m; bad debt provision £4.799m; residential/nursing overspend £4.700m; Supported Living overspend £1.400m; Community Charge income shortfall £3.900m
findings.quote: In summary there was a significant overspend in Children's Social Care services of £27.490m and to a lesser extent in Adults Social Care there was an overspend of £8.818m. It should be noted that this was largely attributable to a year-end bad debt provision charge to the service of £4.799m being made.

findings.paper_title: Performance Monitoring and Budget Monitoring Outturn 2025-26 as at Quarter 4 (31 March 2026)
findings.headline: SEND assessments surged 45% in-year (998 to 1,449 in progress) with timeliness of only 5.7% meeting statutory 20-week target
findings.detail: The SEND service is marked as 'Requiring Action'. EHCP assessments in progress increased from 998 in Q1 to 1,449 in Q4 (45% growth). Only 5.7% of final plans were issued within the 20-week statutory timeframe, though this has improved through the year and the average completion time for Q4 assessments was 26 weeks. The council injected £1.3m one-off investment and is onboarding additional Educational Psychologist locums.
findings.matters: A service marked 'Requiring Action' with massive demand growth and statutory compliance failures (5.7% vs target) indicates governance risk and ongoing spending pressure; the council admits this will remain a 'key improvement priority' for 2026-27.
findings.figures: EHCP assessments in progress increased from 998 (Q1) to 1,449 (Q4); statutory compliance 5.7% against target; average completion time 26 weeks; £1.3m one-off investment provided
findings.quote: This has impacted delivery due to the increased demand for Education Health and Care Plans (EHCP's) with the number of new EHCP assessments in progress increasing from 998 plans at the end of Quarter 1 to 1,449 plans at the end of Quarter 4.

findings.paper_title: Performance Monitoring and Budget Monitoring Outturn 2025-26 as at Quarter 4 (31 March 2026)
findings.headline: Children's Services overspend of £27.5m driven by agency residential placements and EHCP demand spikes
findings.detail: Children's Services overspent by £27.5m (15.9% of budget), with £13.6m on agency residential placements and £4.6m on in-house provision. EHCP costs overran by £4.5m alone. The service is struggling with both supply-side pressures (needing independent/non-maintained providers) and demand growth that is outpacing capacity in maintained schools and academies.
findings.matters: Recurring demand-driven overspends in children's social care are a marker of structural budget imbalance; the council's mitigation strategies (joint funding with health, reducing spot purchases) are not holding the line, signaling escalating costs.
findings.figures: Children's Services overspend £27.490m; agency placements £13.600m; in-house placements £4.600m; EHCP overspend £4.500m; Home to School Transport £4.490m
findings.quote: As previously reported the most significant area of overspend is in Family Help and Children's Social Care provision of homes for children and is primarily on agency residential placements.

findings.paper_title: Performance Monitoring and Budget Monitoring Outturn 2025-26 as at Quarter 4 (31 March 2026)
findings.headline: DSG deficit at £93.3m cumulative, with 10% (£9.3m) remaining unfunded even after government support
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew by £48.6m in-year to reach £93.3m cumulative by March 2026, driven primarily by SEND/EHCP demand. While the government announced it would cover 90% of deficits via Phase 1 funding in 2026-27, this leaves the council facing £9.331m of pressure to fund locally. The report notes that without government intervention this would have put the council 'in an unsustainable position'.
findings.matters: A £9.3m structural deficit liability represents a material contingent risk to reserves and future budget sustainability; it demonstrates demand outstripping government funding in a ring-fenced budget area.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £93.308m at 31 March 2026 (up from £44.737m); in-year deficit £48.571m; High Needs Block overspend £50.724m; residual unfunded pressure £9.331m after Phase 1 support
findings.quote: Without Government intervention, at March 2028 when the regulations were due to expire any deficit on the DSG balances would need to be funded by the Council. This would have put this Council, along with many others, in an unsustainable position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Property Asset Management Strategy 2026-2029
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates structural uncertainty affecting asset and service planning.
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly positions assets in context of pending Local Government Reorganisation, which will move from two-tier to unitary authorities. Year 2 actions include 'reflect and respond to Local Government Reorganisation outcomes', indicating outcomes are not yet known and will shape asset decisions.
findings.matters: LGR will change service delivery structures and revenue bases, potentially making some assets surplus and requiring others. This creates planning uncertainty and risk of stranded capital.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation in Derbyshire will have a significant impact on how services are delivered across the county.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Property Asset Management Strategy 2026-2029
findings.headline: Budget crisis from rising social care costs and real-term funding cuts drove the urgency of this asset management strategy.
findings.detail: The council emerged from COVID responding to 'a significant budget crisis driven by rising social care costs and reductions in real-term budgets'. This is explicitly stated as the context for why asset reviews, disposals, and optimization are happening now, indicating asset strategy is being deployed as a fiscal stabilization tool.
findings.matters: Asset strategy deployed under budget stress signals underlying structural financial problems that require asset disposals and income generation to resolve.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: responding to a significant budget crisis driven by rising social care costs and reductions in real-term budgets

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Property Asset Management Strategy 2026-2029
findings.headline: Energy legislation will mandate capital spending on property upgrades by 2027-2030, adding to existing budget pressure from rising energy costs.
findings.detail: The council identifies rising energy costs as already straining the budget. Additionally, legislation effective April 2027 requires rental commercial properties to meet EPC C rating; this tightens to B rating by April 2030. The council's portfolio includes commercial property subject to these compliance deadlines.
findings.matters: Both current energy costs and future compliance spending create budget pressure. Non-compliance would prevent leasing of properties, affecting income returns.
findings.figures: C rating required April 2027; B rating required April 2030
findings.quote: by April 2027, rented commercial properties will need at least a C rating, and by April 2030, they'll need a B rating to be legally let

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Property Asset Management Strategy 2026-2029
findings.headline: Property data is inconsistent across service areas, undermining the reliability of financial forecasts.
findings.detail: The council states that property data is inconsistent due to piecemeal budget allocation, lack of central accountability, and resource reductions. This makes it difficult to forecast long-term financial impact of asset holdings. The strategy aims to eventually create 25-year cost forecasts, indicating they cannot currently do so reliably.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need to trust asset valuations and lifecycle cost forecasts. Inconsistent data means financial forecasts and balance sheet valuations may be unreliable.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Our property data is inconsistent, as a result of a tendency to focus on the fundamental basics of statutory compliance, the piecemeal allocation of budgets and responsibility for assets across the service areas and the resultant lack of central accountability and the reduction in resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Property Asset Management Strategy 2026-2029
findings.headline: Years of underinvestment in property maintenance have created a backlog that poses financial and service risks.
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges years of underinvestment in maintenance. With increasing extreme weather events (heat, storms, flooding), assets face higher risk of damage if the backlog is not addressed. The portfolio comprises 1,202 sites and over 4,000 assets with a £2.563bn book value.
findings.matters: Maintenance backlog represents a future capital liability and operational risk. Asset failure disrupts services and drives emergency spending.
findings.figures: 1,202 sites, 4,000+ assets, £2.563bn book value
findings.quote: years of underinvestment in property maintenance will result in higher levels of damage to our assets from environmental hazards such as severe heat, storms, and flooding

findings.headline: Planned maintenance programme aims to reduce reactive spend and accumulated backlog liabilities
findings.detail: The strategy shifts from reactive repair spending to whole-life costing and planned maintenance. This approach is framed as reducing both immediate cost volatility and the accumulated backlog of deferred maintenance.
findings.matters: Maintenance backlogs are a hidden liability on council balance sheets; reducing reactive spend improves financial predictability, but no baseline backlog size or remediation timeline is disclosed
findings.figures: No backlog figures or maintenance spending baselines quantified
findings.quote: Whole-life costing and planned maintenance will reduce reactive spend and backlog liabilities.

findings.headline: Commercialisation of surplus assets will generate new income streams
findings.detail: Beyond traditional disposal of redundant property, the council plans to develop commercial revenue from its surplus assets, treating parts of the estate as enterprise income sources rather than service-only infrastructure.
findings.matters: New revenue streams could ease structural budget pressures, but unclear scale and timing mean impact is uncertain until implementation schemes are specific
findings.figures: No quantified income targets provided in this strategy document
findings.quote: Commercialisation of surplus assets will generate new income streams.

findings.headline: Capital receipts from property disposals will support the Medium-Term Financial Plan and reduce borrowing
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly commits to selling property assets as a deliberate financing mechanism. Proceeds will be used to reduce the council's borrowing requirements and alleviate revenue pressures, rather than being treated as contingent returns.
findings.matters: It demonstrates the council's planned reliance on asset sales for debt management and revenue sustainability, directly relevant to refinancing risk and balance sheet trajectory
findings.figures: Estate comprises 1,202 sites and more than 4,000 individual assets with aggregate book value of approximately £2.56bn
findings.quote: Capital receipts from disposals will support the Medium-Term Financial Plan and reduce borrowing in addition to reducing revenue pressures.

findings.headline: Emergency response capabilities degraded; business continuity planning flagged by auditors
findings.detail: The risk 'Failure to respond to emergency situations' is AMBER (12) and was due for completion by 31/12/2025 (now overdue). The register notes this risk was transferred from Place to Corporate Services & Transformation in Q3, with CST now leading work to improve organisational resilience. Internal Audit specifically highlighted business continuity planning as an area for improvement. A new Organisational Resilience Group is being formed to address both this risk and the related 'Failure to deliver critical services in emergency situations' risk.
findings.matters: An overdue emergency response risk combined with auditor feedback on weak business continuity planning raises questions about the council's ability to maintain service delivery during disruption (e.g., cyber incident, major weather event, supply chain failure).
findings.figures: Risk score Amber (12); target completion 31/12/2025 (overdue); financial impact band £3m–£5m; reputation risk High
findings.quote: This risk was transferred from Place to CST during 2025-26 Q3. CST now leads on work to improve the Council's organisational resilience, including business continuity planning which was highlighted by Internal Audit as a specific area for improvement.

findings.headline: Organisational change momentum increased to AMBER due to scale of transformation and weak change readiness
findings.detail: The risk 'Cultural change does not keep pace with transformation' moved from GREEN (6) to AMBER (12) in Q3. The register attributes this to significant organisational change on the horizon through the One Council Operating Model Transformation and LGR, combined with need to strengthen change management and understand the organisation's readiness for change. Further work is needed on colleague and stakeholder engagement. Financial impact is Band 7 (£10m–£20m).
findings.matters: Moving to AMBER signals the council believes transformation momentum is outpacing cultural readiness. This typically precedes delays, rework, staff turnover, and programme slippage. Band 7 financial impact suggests the transformation spend itself is material.
findings.figures: Risk score moved from Green (6) to Amber (12) in Q3 2025-26; financial impact band £10m–£20m; target Green by 31/08/26
findings.quote: This risk has moved to Amber. Significant organisational change is on the horizon through the One Council Operating Model Transformation and Local Government Reorganisation (LGR). Further work is required to strengthen change management and understand the organisations readiness for change, with particular focus on colleague and stakeholder engagement.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation creating resource drain and service continuity risk
findings.detail: LGR preparation will consume management time and resources leading up to vesting day of the new unitary councils in Derbyshire. This new risk is AMBER (12) with a target of GREEN (9) by 31/05/26. The council submitted its 'Uniting Derbyshire' proposal in November 2025 for a single county unitary. The register flags risk of disruption to services and functions on transition, with financial impact band £100k–£1m but reputation risk flagged as High.
findings.matters: Large-scale reorganisations divert management bandwidth, freeze decision-making, and create uncertainty. A lender needs to know whether the council can maintain service delivery and financial discipline through this disruption, and what the new entity's financial model will be.
findings.figures: Risk score Amber (12); target Green by 31/05/26; financial impact band £100k–£1m; reputation risk High
findings.quote: Work to prepare for LGR will consume management time and other resources which could impact on the ongoing delivery of statutory and other functions by the County Council leading up to vesting day of the unitary councils in Derbyshire.

findings.headline: Contract management risk overdue by 2.5 years with no resolution date
findings.detail: The risk 'Failure to manage contracts across the county council' was due for completion on 19/09/2023 and remains AMBER (12). The register notes it is under review as part of a review of the Procurement risk register, with no new completion date provided. Financial impact is Band 8 (£20m+). Failure to manage contracts effectively could lead to unforeseen costs, contract collapse, or increased carbon footprint.
findings.matters: An overdue risk under review for 2.5 years with no completion date signals either controls are ineffective or the scope is unmanageable. Band 8 financial impact means major supplier failure could be material.
findings.figures: Target completion 19/09/2023 (overdue); financial impact band £20m+; risk score Amber (12)
findings.quote: Failure to manage contracts across the county council (19/09/2023). Both risks are currently subject to a fundamental review... Risk under review.

findings.headline: Highways asset maintenance underfunded despite EMCCA funding boost
findings.detail: The council faces sustained need for investment in highways assets to meet the Code of Practice for Well-Managed Highway Infrastructure. Although EMCCA funding has increased the 2025-26 programme from ~£40m to £70m, the register notes that issues like landslips, retaining walls, and ageing structures cannot be addressed in the short term within current budgets. Risk remains AMBER (12) against a GREEN (9) target. The risk owner plans to seek EMCCA agreement for long-term sustained investment.
findings.matters: Highways are critical infrastructure. Underfunding has already created a backlog, and the council is now dependent on external (EMCCA) funding to arrest decline. If EMCCA funding changes, the backlog will resume growing.
findings.figures: 2025-26 investment £70m (vs ~£40m in prior years); financial impact band £1m–£3m; risk score Amber (12)
findings.quote: Issues such as landslips, retaining walls and ageing structures cannot all be addressed in the short-term or within current budgets... Maintaining highway assets to the required standard needs sustained investment over the longer term.

findings.headline: Property maintenance backlog growing as budget cuts force deferral of non-statutory work
findings.detail: The risk owner reports that reducing budget impacts the ability to undertake maintenance, with focus narrowed to statutory compliance and essential H&S work. As a result, overall building condition is deteriorating and the maintenance backlog is increasing despite the number of assets reducing. Risk is AMBER (12) against a GREEN (9) target.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance is an unfunded liability that grows over time. A council deferring everything but statutory work signals constrained capital, and deteriorating assets raise long-term cost risk.
findings.figures: Financial impact band £1m–£3m; risk score Amber (12); target Green by 01/04/26
findings.quote: Reducing budget impacts ability to undertake maintenance, focus remains on statutory compliance and essential H&S related maintenance leading to overall building condition deteriorating and maintenance backlog increasing, even though number of assets is reducing.

findings.headline: Special educational needs budget deficit of £6m with demand surging 140% in six years
findings.detail: The council's SEND service faces a budget deficit of over £6m (as of June 2024) driven by Education, Health and Care Plans surging from 3,666 in 2019 to 8,801 in 2025. The risk is AMBER with a target completion date of 30/09/26. The national SEND deficit is £4.6bn, and the register notes this contributes to the risk of two-fifths of local authorities issuing a Section 114 notice by March 2026.
findings.matters: This is structural demand growth the council cannot control. A £6m deficit on a growing baseline is material and ongoing. The March 2026 accounting override cliff is mentioned as relevant to Section 114 decisions across the sector.
findings.figures: £6m+ deficit; EHCPs 3,666 (2019) to 8,801 (2025); demand increase 140%; national deficit £4.6bn
findings.quote: The council's budget deficit for EHCPs and HTST is over £6m (June 2024)... There is a national financial deficit estimated at £4.6bn contributing in part to the risk of two-fifths of local authorities issuing a Section 114 notice by March 2026 when the accounting statutory override ends.

findings.headline: Revenue budget deficit of £1.38m persisting through Q1 and Q2
findings.detail: The council's risk register shows ongoing pressure on operating within available funding, with a revenue forecast outturn of £1.38m in both Q1 and Q2. This risk remains at AMBER (15) against a target of GREEN (9), meaning identified controls are not sufficient to bring spending in line with income.
findings.matters: A persistent deficit signals either budget assumptions are wrong or service costs are not under control. Lenders need to know whether the council has exhausted reserves or has a credible plan to balance.
findings.figures: £1.38m revenue forecast outturn; risk score 15 against target of 9
findings.quote: Q2 revenue forecast outturn similar to Q1 at £1.38m.

findings.headline: 28% of new capital investment (£27.5m of £96.5m) now funded by borrowing, with zero capital receipts from asset sales
findings.detail: The council's new capital starts for 2026-27 total £96.545m, financed as follows: £69.010m grants (71%), £27.535m borrowing (29%), £0.000m capital receipts (0%). The council has no capital receipts (proceeds from asset sales) to fund new investment, meaning every pound of capital spending beyond grant funding must come from borrowing. The strategy notes that the council previously used revenue funding for capital but states 'the impact growing demand and cost pressures on the Council's revenue budget has reduced options in this area.'
findings.matters: Capital receipts and revenue contributions provide financial flexibility independent of debt markets and grant availability. Their absence means the council must borrow for every pound of discretionary capital, increasing debt and reducing flexibility to respond to service emergencies or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: New capital starts 2026-27: £96.545m total; financing: grants £69.010m (71%), borrowing £27.535m (29%), capital receipts £0.000m (0%)
findings.quote: However, the impact growing demand and cost pressures on the Council's revenue budget has reduced options in this area.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement (outstanding debt) growing at 20x the annual repayment rate—from £717.7m to £851.8m over five years
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (total outstanding capital debt not yet permanently financed) is forecast to grow from £717.656m in 2024-25 to £851.756m in 2028-29, an increase of £134.1m. Against this, Minimum Revenue Provision (the annual repayment) is only £13.8-15.3m. The council is accumulating debt far faster than it is repaying it, creating a long-tail repayment obligation stretching decades into the future.
findings.matters: Accelerating debt accumulation indicates weakening debt sustainability. The council will need sustained revenue resources to repay this growing debt, reducing financial flexibility if service demands or financing costs rise further.
findings.figures: CFR 2024-25: £717.656m → 2028-29: £851.756m (growth of £134.1m or 18.7%); MRP 2026-27: £14.340m (less than 11% of the year's CFR growth)
findings.quote: Where the Council finances capital expenditure from borrowing, it must put aside resources to repay that debt in later years. The amount charged to the revenue budget for the repayment of debt is known as Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP).

findings.headline: Council's capital financing costs projected to rise 11% while acknowledging 'unprecedented' revenue budget pressures from social care and SEN demand
findings.detail: Financing costs (interest and debt repayment) are set to increase from £42.423m in 2024-25 to £47.107m in 2027-28. The council explicitly states it faces 'unprecedented pressures' on revenue from rising service costs, cost-of-living impacts, and growing demand for adult social care, children's social care, and special educational needs. The Strategy acknowledges that 'any decisions to fund capital investment from borrowing must carefully consider the revenue budget implications for future years,' suggesting awareness that debt service growth may become unsustainable.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the council's revenue growth can support both escalating service costs and rising debt service. If revenue lags cost growth, debt service will crowd out service spending, and the council may struggle to service borrowed funds.
findings.figures: Financing costs £42.423m (2024-25) → £47.107m (2027-28), a £4.684m (11%) increase. Financing costs as % of net revenue excluding DSG: 5.82% (2024-25) → 5.43% (2028-29), with absolute costs rising
findings.quote: In the context of growing cost and demand pressures on the revenue budget, any decisions to fund capital investment from borrowing must carefully consider the revenue budget implications for future years.

findings.headline: Council Tax at maximum increase (4.9%) with future years also planned at maximum, leaving no flexibility
findings.detail: The Council is increasing Council Tax by the maximum permitted 4.9% (2.99% general plus 2% Adult Social Care precept) to raise an additional £24.103m. The paper explicitly states that 'future Council Tax increases in the current medium term financial plan (MTFP) for future years have been assumed at the maximum allowed', removing any flexibility to respond to emerging pressures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council has exhausted its Council Tax lever already and has no headroom to respond to further financial pressures during the multi-year settlement.
findings.figures: 4.9% increase; additional £24.103m; only 0.57% taxbase growth
findings.quote: Increasing Council Tax by 4.9% will raise around an additional £24.103m in Council Tax income in 2026-27 and future years to support the Council's vital services.

findings.headline: Business Rates Revaluation yields zero growth and forecloses £2m pool share, with estimates not finalised until 31 January
findings.detail: The Business Rates Revaluation (effective 1 April 2026) is expected to deliver zero or very little growth. Consequently, there will be no share from the Derbyshire Business Rates Pool of £2.000m in 2026-27. Final business rates estimates from billing authorities are not due until 31 January 2026, after the Council has set its budget, and 'could change', to be managed through reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that a material and volatile income stream has stalled, and the Council's budget rests on income assumptions not confirmed until after formal budget adoption.
findings.figures: Business Rates Pool: £2.000m (not received); Local business rates estimate: £22.563m
findings.quote: Due to a Business Rates Revaluation, the Districts and Boroughs have declared that there will be zero or very little growth and so there won't be any share from the Derbyshire Business Rates Pool of £2.000m in 2026-27.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection fund surplus of only £0.2m, with multiple district deficits and late confirmation
findings.detail: The total Council Tax collection fund surplus is forecast at just £0.203m for 2026-27. Several individual districts show deficits: Derbyshire Dales -£742k, High Peak -£420k, and Amber Valley -£64k. Because billing authorities do not confirm their final collection fund positions until 31 January 2026 (after this Council sets its budget), material variances could emerge.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the Council has minimal buffer for collection variations or economic shocks, and key income assumptions are not finalised until after budget-setting.
findings.figures: £0.203m surplus; Derbyshire Dales deficit £742k; High Peak deficit £420k; Amber Valley deficit £64k
findings.quote: The total Council Tax collection fund surplus for 2026-27 is estimated at £0.203m, based on information received from billing authorities.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care pressures of £34.7m exceed new government funding, with 4.1% wage cost increase
findings.detail: The Council faces £34.693m of ASC cost pressures in 2026-27. Meanwhile, the National Living Wage is rising 4.1% (from £12.21 to £12.71 from April 2026), adding substantial pressure to pay budgets and contracts in social care. Although £150m of the £900m new national ASC funding rolls in for 2026-27, the Council is relying on maximum Council Tax increases to bridge the gap.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can absorb cost growth in its largest and most volatile service area, where wages are rising faster than government funding.
findings.figures: £34.693m ASC pressures; National Living Wage up from £12.21 to £12.71 (4.1% increase)
findings.quote: There are substantial demands on the Council's services, in particular, social care where for ASC pressures for 2026-27 are £34.693m.

findings.headline: Funding reforms specifically disadvantage Derbyshire, realllocating £600m away and removing rural cost recognition
findings.detail: Local Government Reform is targeted at low-taxbase/high-deprivation authorities, causing a 'significant reallocation of funding... to the detriment of funding for Derbyshire County Council.' Additionally, the Remoteness Factor used to recognise that rural services cost more to run has been removed from funding calculations (except for Adult Social Care only), meaning rural costs are no longer acknowledged in funding allocations. Derbyshire also does not receive a new Recovery Grant Guarantee being introduced for other upper tier authorities.
findings.matters: The council faces structural funding headwinds over the entire three-year multi-year settlement period, with no mechanism to recover rural cost disadvantage.
findings.figures: £600m Recovery Grant reallocated; Derbyshire ineligible for Recovery Grant Guarantee
findings.quote: Local Government Reform will bring about a significant reallocation of funding with it being targeted at low taxbase/high deprivation authorities. The £600m Recovery Grant Remains in place throughout the MYS. This will be to the detriment of funding for Derbyshire County Council.

findings.headline: Council has accumulated £84m SEND deficit with government support still unannounced
findings.detail: The Council faces an estimated SEND deficit of £84m at the end of March 2026. The government has stated that from March 2028 (end of Statutory Override), local authorities will not be expected to use general funds to cover SEND deficits, but it has not yet announced details of how it will support councils with accrued deficits. Final guidance is expected only by early February 2026, after this budget is set.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that this council has a massive accumulated liability with unknown settlement terms, which constrains financial flexibility and may require drawing down reserves or borrowing.
findings.figures: £84m estimated deficit at March 2026
findings.quote: The Government has recognised that local authorities will need support for the accrued deficits. Details of this support has not yet been announced but may be released as part of the Final LGFS expected in early February. The Council's estimated deficit at the end of March 2026 is c.£84m.

findings.headline: Total investment portfolio forecast to contract 56% over two years, from £130.351m to £56.674m
findings.detail: The council's total investment exposure (treasury management, pooled funds, and service loans) is forecast to fall from £130.351m in March 2025 to £56.674m in March 2027. Service loans alone will decline from £15.514m to £0.321m. Treasury management investments will drop to £10.000m, the minimum balance required for MIFID professional status.
findings.matters: A 56% portfolio contraction over two years is material and suggests either a strategic shift to reduce investment risk exposure or financial pressure requiring asset liquidation; the document does not explain which.
findings.figures: Total investment exposure: £130.351m (March 2025) to £56.674m (March 2027); Service loans: £15.514m to £0.321m
findings.quote: TOTAL INVESTMENTS 130.351 69.881 56.674

findings.headline: £11.390m Buxton Crescent Hotel loan fully repaid from sale proceeds in December 2025
findings.detail: The council's largest service investment loan was repaid in full on 5 December 2025 when the hotel operators sold the business as a going concern. This represents an exit from the council's major commercial property investment.
findings.matters: Exit from a major commercial loan signals portfolio rebalancing or recognition that the investment strategy required adjustment; the characterisation as a 'going concern' sale suggests the loan was repaid from operational proceeds rather than distressed liquidation.
findings.figures: £11.390m repayment on 5 December 2025
findings.quote: The hotel was sold as a going concern by the hotel operators on 5 December 2025. The original loan of £11.390m was repaid from the sale proceeds.

findings.headline: Council approves zero new lending to Local Regeneration Partners, signalling exit from category with 32% loss provisioning
findings.detail: The approved limit for Local Regeneration Partners loans for 2026-27 is Nil. As of 31 March 2025, the council held £15.117m in outstanding loans to this category with a £4.866m loss allowance, reducing the net figure to £10.251m. The move to Nil suggests deliberate withdrawal from an investment category carrying significant credit risk.
findings.matters: Loss allowances at 32% of outstanding balance suggest either deteriorating borrower credit quality or aggressive provisioning against expected defaults; an exit from such investments reduces exposure to credit risk but may also indicate problem loans.
findings.figures: £15.117m balance owed, £4.866m loss allowance, Nil approved limit 2026-27
findings.quote: Local Regeneration Partners 15.117 -4.866 10.251 Nil

findings.headline: 90% of the council's one-off savings (£6.7m of £7.433m) is government grant income, not sustainable council savings
findings.detail: The Extended Producer Responsibility Income of £6.700m is explicitly identified as 'not a saving but Government grant income to cover expenditure which the Council would have otherwise had to fund'. This means the council's financial plan for 2026-27 depends heavily on government grant continuation outside its control.
findings.matters: Grant-dependent savings are vulnerable to withdrawal or reduction by government, creating unforecast funding gaps if the grant ceases or is reduced
findings.figures: £6.700m of £7.433m one-off savings (90%) is government EPR grant income
findings.quote: This is not a saving but Government grant income to cover expenditure which the Council would have otherwise had to fund

findings.headline: Council is deferring statutory Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) debt repayment in 2026-27
findings.detail: The council is treating a £4.241m deferral of MRP contribution as a cost saving, explicitly to 'offset loss of cash to invest'. MRP is the statutory mechanism for repaying borrowing over time. Deferring this contribution preserves cash for current spending but leaves debt repayment obligations unmet.
findings.matters: Non-payment of statutory debt repayment obligations suggests capital programme or cash flow constraints and may flag refinancing pressures
findings.figures: £4.241m saving from deferral of MRP contribution
findings.quote: Contribution to offset loss in cash to invest not being made

findings.headline: Council is using reserves to offset payroll pressure rather than reducing payroll costs
findings.detail: The council plans to deploy £5.416m of brought-forward balance to offset payroll pressure in 2026-27. This is a one-off measure that depletes the emergency reserve without addressing underlying payroll cost levels, indicating the council cannot reduce payroll through normal savings processes.
findings.matters: Using reserves to cover current operational costs signals structural budget problems and erodes the financial buffer available for emergencies or unexpected shocks
findings.figures: £5.416m brought-forward balance allocated to payroll pressure offset
findings.quote: Brought forward balance that can be used to offset payroll pressure

findings.headline: Shire county faces structural funding decline over the next three years
findings.detail: The council is subject to major funding reforms that will progressively reduce shire county funding allocations. The £55.332m savings programme (£47.898m ongoing, £7.433m one-off) is designed to bridge the resulting funding gap. The council assumes no further major funding reductions from 2029-30 onwards, but this carries execution risk if government policy changes.
findings.matters: A council facing structural income decline combined with aggressive multi-year savings targets represents elevated refinancing and budgetary risk
findings.figures: £55.332m total savings required; £47.898m ongoing; £7.433m one-off; savings profile 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.quote: major funding reforms which will see, as a Shire County, Derbyshire's level of funding reduce over the next 3 years

findings.headline: Investment income (£3.2m) will cover only one-fifth of debt interest costs (£16.5m) in 2026-27
findings.detail: The council budgets for £16.497m in debt interest costs but only £3.205m in investment income, a deficit of £13.3m annually. This gap is typical for borrowing councils, but the income is concentrated in strategic pooled funds (£2.2m of the £3.2m) which carry market risk and volatility, making investment income unreliable.
findings.matters: A reliance on volatile investment returns to offset a portion of debt costs means revenue budgets are exposed to investment market performance. Any downturn in pooled fund valuations or wider market stress could reduce income below the budget assumption.
findings.figures: Debt interest budget 2026-27: £16.497m; investment income budget: £3.205m; strategic pooled funds income: £2.200m from £50m at 4.40% yield
findings.quote: The budget for investment income in 2026-27 is £3.205m, based on an income of £0.605m from traditional investments, £2.200m from £50.000m nominal of strategic pooled funds at an interest rate of 4.40% and £0.400m from other dividends.

findings.headline: Capital programme has a documented history of significant delivery slippage
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states that past experience shows a high probability of slippage in capital project delivery. For a council with a Capital Financing Requirement growing from £717.7m to £851.8m over four years, slippage means planned capital investment may not be completed on schedule, potentially affecting service outcomes and the timing of the borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays call into question whether borrowing forecasts are realistic and whether planned capital investment will actually deliver expected service improvements or revenue benefits that justify the cost of borrowing.
findings.figures: CFR growing from £717.656m (31.3.25) to £851.756m (31.3.29); additional external borrowing required to fund capital programme forecast at £222m+ annually
findings.quote: Past experience has demonstrated a high probability of slippage in delivery of the Capital Programme.

findings.headline: Schools funding deficit of £48.9m is being financed through short-term borrowing
findings.detail: The council is carrying a Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit of £48.871m, which is being funded through short-term external borrowing. This represents accumulated deficits in school funding that the council must cover from its general fund, creating an ongoing drain on resources that is not self-resolving.
findings.matters: A structural deficit in schools funding indicates either inadequate DSG allocations for the council's school population or budget management issues within the education service. This deficit will continue to consume council resources unless schools funding improves or spending is reduced.
findings.figures: DSG deficit funded by short-term borrowing: £48.871m
findings.quote: Short-term borrowing includes £48.871m for funding the Council's DSG deficit.

findings.headline: Usable reserves will fall by over 60%, from £323.6m to £105.2m over four years
findings.detail: The council's usable reserves are forecast to decline from £323.578m in March 2025 to just £105.225m by March 2029. This £218m reduction over four years reflects the council drawing down reserves to fund operations and capital investment. At this rate, reserves will be depleted to less than a third of current levels, severely limiting financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion reduces the council's capacity to absorb shocks or manage unexpected pressures, and indicates reliance on drawing down accumulated assets rather than achieving sustainable revenue balance.
findings.quote: This level of investment is expected to fall significantly in subsequent years as short-term external borrowing is repaid and internal reserves are utilised.

findings.headline: Council will borrow an additional £222m in 2026-27, with £432.9m new borrowing needed by 2029
findings.detail: The council currently holds £413.9m of borrowing. The balance sheet forecast shows the council will borrow up to £222m in 2026-27 alone, reaching £432.9m of cumulative new borrowing by March 2029. This represents a substantial increase in the council's total debt position over the forecast period as it funds its capital programme.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the council can service this level of additional debt from its revenue streams and whether the capital projects being funded will generate sufficient returns or service improvements to justify the borrowing cost.
findings.figures: Current borrowing: £413.929m (31 Dec 2025); new borrowing 2026-27: £222.046m; cumulative new borrowing by 2029: £432.882m
findings.quote: The Council expects to borrow up to an additional £222.046m in 2026-27.

findings.headline: Planned income loss of £1.026m following corporate decision already made
findings.detail: The council has already made a corporate decision that will result in an income stream in Corporate Services and Transformation ceasing at some point in 2026-27. A contingency budget is held against this known loss.
findings.matters: Known income loss that reduces financial flexibility and reflects strategic business model changes.
findings.quote: This is a centrally Corporate Contingency Budget, which is being held as a prudent measure in case an income stream in the Corporate Services and Transformation department ceases at some point in 2026-27, following a Corporate decision which has already been made.

findings.headline: Council exiting Disability Design Team discretionary service to District and Boroughs
findings.detail: The council has decided to cease delivering a discretionary service and exit fully by end of March 2026, with consultation on funding top-ups. This creates a £0.505m budget pressure from lost income.
findings.matters: Strategic service withdrawal affecting partner councils; signals shift in council's service model and income sources.
findings.quote: The Council has taken the decision to cease delivering the discretionary service for the District and Boroughs and to consult on funding top ups. The Council is expected to exit the service fully at the end of March 2026.

findings.headline: Council sold three of seven pooled investment funds in January 2025, reducing interest income base
findings.detail: The council disposed of three pooled investment funds, reducing the 2026-27 interest and dividend income budget by £1.0m. While this generates £599k additional interest on cash, the net effect is a £0.401m budget pressure.
findings.matters: Indicates the council has taken action to manage cash position and signals reduced investment income base going forward.
findings.figures: £1.000m reduction in investment income, £0.599m offset by cash interest, £0.401m net pressure
findings.quote: The 2026-27 budget has been reduced by £1.000m due to the Council having sold three out of seven of its pooled investment funds in January 2025.

findings.headline: Pay award contingency of £10.007m at risk if actual award exceeds 3.5% assumption
findings.detail: The council holds £10.007m contingency pending the actual pay award announcement. If the award exceeds the 3.5% assumption, additional cost must come from within existing budgets or be managed using reserves.
findings.matters: Material budget risk with explicit acknowledgement that any overspend forces in-year cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £10.007m contingency, 3.5% assumption
findings.quote: If the pay award is agreed at a level above this, the additional cost will have to be found from within existing budgets or managed using reserves.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demographic pressures of £6.755m from aging population and working-age complexity growth
findings.detail: Ongoing pressures include £3.2m from projected growth in the 75+ population and those with dementia, and £3.555m from increased numbers of adults with disabilities and complexity, including young adults transitioning from children's services.
findings.matters: Structural demographic trends that will not reverse and indicate a growing baseline cost that the council's savings plans must overcome.
findings.figures: £3.200m (65+), £3.555m (working age), £6.755m total
findings.quote: Underlying demographic growth pressures remain in Adult Care. Predictive factors for these pressures include projected increases in the 75+ population, people living alone, in poor housing, with relative financial deprivation, with one or more health conditions or with dementia.

findings.headline: SEND home to school transport demand pressure of £6.644m, with £3.8m from unbudgeted existing demand
findings.detail: The council faces £3.8m pressure just to meet existing SEND transport demand that exceeded previous budget estimates, plus an additional £2.844m for forecast growth linked to rising EHCP identification.
findings.matters: Shows another major service where actual cost is outrunning budget, with growth driven by statutory EHCP obligations the council must meet.
findings.figures: £3.800m existing demand, £2.844m additional demand, £6.644m total
findings.quote: To meet the existing demand for SEND home to school transport. This reflects the demand related growth which was in excess of previous years' budget estimates.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care carrying £2m unfunded cost from delays in prior-years' savings initiatives
findings.detail: The council did not deliver savings it had planned in Adult Social Care in prior years. The £2m pressure now funds the impact of these delays and reflects an underlying departmental overspend from November 2025.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings is a delivery/governance risk that affects budget credibility and forecast accuracy.
findings.quote: To fund the impact of delays in implementing prior years' savings initiatives. This pressure reflects the department's underlying overspend based on the November 2025 forecast position.

findings.headline: Children's placements already exceeding budget by £14m before forecasting additional demand
findings.detail: The council faces £14m pressure just to meet existing placement demand that outran previous budget estimates, plus an additional £3.233m for forecast growth. This reflects unbudgeted cost of existing caseload, not just future growth.
findings.matters: Shows the council's budget cycle is failing to accurately forecast children in care costs, and underlying caseload is more expensive than planned. This is a service the council cannot legally reduce.
findings.figures: £14.000m existing demand, £3.233m forecast additional demand, £17.233m total
findings.quote: To meet the existing demand for placements for children in care and 'in care' alternatives. This reflects the demand related growth which was in excess of previous years' budget estimates.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves forecast to decline by £31m over four years, with £13.8m grant transfer anticipated by March 2026
findings.detail: Non-schools earmarked reserves are forecast to fall from £159m (March 2025) to £128m (March 2029). The £13.812m Bus Services Improvement Grant is anticipated to transfer to the East Midlands Combined County Authority when transport functions transfer before 31 March 2026, representing a significant loss of earmarked resources.
findings.matters: As reserves deplete, the council loses financial flexibility to absorb unexpected costs or service pressures. The grant transfer timeline is not certain ('anticipated'), creating additional uncertainty about the 2026 reserves position.
findings.figures: £159m (31 March 2025) declining to £128m (31 March 2029); £13.812m Bus Services grant transfer
findings.quote: Excluding schools' balances, Earmarked Reserves balances are forecast to reduce from £159m at 31 March 2025 to £128m by 31 March 2029.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges three-year reliance on reserves to manage budget pressures is unsustainable
findings.detail: From 2022-23 to 2024-25, Derbyshire drew down reserves to cover inflationary, demand, and pay pressures, using £18.879m in 2024-25 alone. The council explicitly states this approach is 'not sustainable' and signals that future budget pressures must be managed through savings proposals instead, not reserves.
findings.matters: This reveals the council has been deferring structural budget problems using one-off reserves rather than finding sustainable savings. Once reserves deplete further, the council will face genuine budget pressures with no safety net.
findings.figures: £18.879m used in 2024-25; reliance spanning 2022-23 to 2024-25
findings.quote: Reserves cannot be relied upon to support future years' spending. From 2022-23 to 2024-25, the Council utilised its reserves to manage its budget to meet inflationary, demand and pay award cost pressures; however, this is not sustainable.

findings.headline: Pay award costs £10m in 2026-27 with government support only partial and rolled into baseline funding
findings.detail: The council faces 3.5% pay award across all pay points in 2026-27 and future years, costing approximately £10m annually. Employer National Insurance contribution support was provided separately in 2025-26 but has been rolled into Revenue Support Grant for 2026-27, meaning government support no longer fully offsets the cost increase.
findings.matters: Loss of ringfenced funding means base pressures absorb more of general grant; cost of pay awards is now less transparent and harder to fund.
findings.figures: £10m annual pay award cost; 3.5% increase assumed across all pay points
findings.quote: It is estimated that the pay award will cost the Council around £10m in 2026-27. The direct cost increase in the Employer National Insurance contributions will be partly supported again by grant from the Government, but it has been rolled into the RSG. It will not fully cover the additional cost as was the case in 2025-26.

findings.headline: Council Tax increase to maximum 4.9% required to maximize Core Spending Power and support financial sustainability
findings.detail: The council is recommending the maximum allowable Council Tax increase (ASC Precept 1.99% plus basic 3% = 4.9%) to maximize government-calculated Core Spending Power. The S151 officer notes this is 'the single most effective way of providing a base budget to support the delivery of services and maintain financial sustainability over the longer term,' but acknowledges this occurs 'at a time when many households will be struggling.'
findings.matters: Maximum Council Tax increases are a limited resource; at-maximum increases signal limited flexibility for future years and limited headroom from political pressure.
findings.figures: 4.9% total increase (ASC Precept 1.99% + basic Council Tax 3.00%)
findings.quote: This report recommends that the Council accepts the need to levy a total increase of 4.9% (an ASC Precept increase of 1.99% and a basic Council Tax increase of 3.00%), which is the maximum allowed and therefore the Council's maximise its CSP.

findings.headline: Forward budget years increasingly difficult to balance; ability to set balanced budget across MTFP period is 'a concern'
findings.detail: While 2026-27 can be balanced, the S151 officer explicitly states: 'the ability to set a balanced budget across the period of the MTFP is a concern as pressures are expected to continue and the Council's allocated funding in the multi-year settlement reduces over the 3 years.' The document emphasizes 'Tough decisions will need to be taken and planning needs to start as soon as possible.'
findings.matters: Medium-term sustainability is uncertain; a lender cannot assume the council will successfully navigate the 2027-28 and 2028-29 budget positions.
findings.figures: MTFP covers 2026-27 to 2030-31; settlement covers 2026-27 to 2028-29 with funding reductions; 0.5% DEL cut from 2028-29
findings.quote: However, the ability to set a balanced budget across the period of the MTFP is a concern as pressures are expected to continue and the Council's allocated funding in the multi-year settlement reduces over the 3 years. Tough decisions will need to be taken and planning needs to start as soon as possible to achieve this.

findings.headline: Section 114 notice risk rising: 14 issued since 1988, 11 in the last seven years
findings.detail: The document notes that since 2018 there have been 11 Section 114 notices issued (compared to 1 between 2000-2018), indicating accelerating financial failure across the sector. The S151 officer identifies this as a forward risk: 'If the budget cannot be balanced through finding savings and the need to use substantial amounts of reserves, then the Chief Finance Officer will as a last resort have to issue a Section 114.'
findings.matters: A lender must consider whether Derbyshire has sufficient savings pipeline and reserve depth to avoid joining this accelerating trend of councils in financial difficulty.
findings.figures: 14 Section 114 notices issued since 1988; 11 issued since 2018; rising frequency from 1 in 18 years to 11 in 7 years
findings.quote: There have been 14 Section 114 notices issued since the Local Government Finance Act 1988 became law. Hillingdon and Hackney councils were the first and second to do so, in 2000. Then the next one wasn't issued until 2018. Since then, there have been 11 more Section 114s issued.

findings.headline: External auditor's positive judgment on financial stability is conditional on achievement of savings and reserve maintenance
findings.detail: The council's auditor continues to report positively on financial stability, but only 'subject to the continuing achievement of budget savings and the upkeep of a robust, risk assessed level of reserves.' This conditionality signals auditor concern about sustainability if either condition fails.
findings.matters: Conditional audit opinion is a red flag; lenders track auditor language closely as an early warning signal of deteriorating financial resilience.
findings.figures: Auditor judgment 'continues to be positive subject to' two conditions
findings.quote: The external auditor makes a judgement on the financial stability of the Council each year when the accounts are audited and also performs a Value For Money (VFM) Assessment. The judgement continues to be positive subject to the continuing achievement of budget savings and the upkeep of a robust, risk assessed level of reserves.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care faces annual demographic cost growth of £7.5-8m plus National Living Wage rises adding up to £10m annually
