findings.detail: Demographic growth drives annual increases of £4-5m for older people and £3.5m for working-age adults. Additionally, National Living Wage increases (4.1% for 2026-26) directly impact care provider contract fees, estimated at up to £10m annually. These pressures are predicted to continue for at least five years.
findings.matters: Structural demographic and wage-inflation pressures that cannot be controlled by the council; lenders assess sustainability against uncontrollable cost drivers.
findings.figures: £8m annual demographic cost growth; 4.1% National Living Wage increase 2026-26; up to £10m annual impact from care provider fee increases
findings.quote: Growth predictions show that the Council is subject to approximate annual increases of up to £4-5m in relation to older people demography, with a further £3.5m for working age adults including children transitioning to adulthood. These additional costs of up to £8m each year are predicted to continue for at least the next five years.

findings.headline: £41.1m additional pressure in Children's Services with demand showing no sign of slowing
findings.detail: Children's Services faces £41.079m in pressures for 2026-27 (including £10.595m pay/price inflation and £30.484m ongoing service pressure). The S151 officer notes 'the continuing upward trend of these pressures is a major concern and put the Council's financial sustainability at risk over the medium term.' Recent AGS notes 'material increase in demand for children's care which shows no sign of slowing down.'
findings.matters: Demand-led services without corresponding funding growth create structural budget gaps; lenders need confidence the council can manage or contain this trajectory.
findings.figures: £41.079m Children's Services pressures in 2026-27; demographic-driven growth continues across MTFP period
findings.quote: There are significant pressures in several areas which are well documented and discussed. The pressures are recognised by the Government as an issue nationally. The pressures have been identified and included in the MTFP. The continuing upward trend of these pressures is a major concern and put the Council's financial sustainability at risk over the medium term.

findings.headline: Funding reductions phased in over 3-year settlement, with major shift away from shire counties
findings.detail: The 2026-27 multi-year settlement is the first in over a decade, but Derbyshire's allocated funding reduces over the three years as government implements reforms. New funding formula targets high-deprivation areas and removes remoteness indicator, disadvantaging shire counties. This structural reallocation will require 'tough decisions' beginning immediately.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that Derbyshire faces structural income decline regardless of savings delivery, compounding the difficulty of balancing forward budgets.
findings.quote: The Council's funding reduces over the 3 years as the Government introduces its reforms one third at a time over the 3 years. It allows time to plan for the redirection of funding to those areas of highest deprivation which will be to the detriment of shire counties.

findings.headline: £84.6m SEND deficit will become unfunded liability when statutory override expires in March 2028
findings.detail: Derbyshire faces a projected DSG deficit of £84.603m by end of 2025-26 arising from unfunded SEND expenditure over several years. The statutory override allowing this to be held separately expires 31 March 2028, at which point the deficit must be funded by the council. Nationally, the sector faces a £14bn cumulative deficit, and sector surveys suggest most councils would be unable to set a balanced budget without government intervention.
findings.matters: This represents a deferred liability that will hit the council's balance sheet unless government provides a solution; it threatens financial sustainability and ability to borrow.
findings.figures: £84.603m; £14bn national cumulative deficit; £3m annually estimated revenue cost for Derbyshire if borrowing required
findings.quote: By March 2026, Derbyshire County Council is forecast to hold approximately £84m of additional debt arising from unfunded expenditure on statutory Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) services over several years. This represents one of the Council's most significant financial risks

findings.headline: £2.587m of £37.499m planned savings (6.9%) rated Red with significant delivery risk
findings.detail: Of the council's £37.499m savings target, 93.1% is forecast as delivered or on track (Green/Amber), but £2.587m remains Red-rated with significant risks. Departments are developing alternative proposals to cover at-risk savings.
findings.matters: The £1.612m headline overspend already requires mitigation. If Red-rated savings fail, the problem grows by £2.587m (160% larger). This is identified financial planning risk.
findings.figures: £2.587m Red-rated; £37.499m total target; 6.9% at risk; 93.1% on track
findings.quote: £2.587m of savings (6.9% of the original target) are rated Red i.e. there are significant risks to delivery and therefore the forecast does not therefore assume these will be delivered.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to reach £84.603m cumulatively by 31 March 2026, £40.201m of it from High Needs Block in 2025-26 alone
findings.detail: The DSG in-year deficit is £39.756m in 2025-26, accumulating to £84.603m total. Currently held separately under a government override (extended to March 2028), but the government has not yet addressed treatment of historic deficits. The document notes Section 151 Officers warned that if required to recognise deficits in revenue accounts, it would 'bankrupt many local authorities' requiring Section 114 notices.
findings.matters: This is a latent liability. While ring-fenced now, the override expires in 2028 with no government clarity on whether councils must absorb these losses. An £84m deficit converting to General Fund would be catastrophic. This is a political and solvency risk.
findings.figures: £39.756m in-year deficit 2025-26; £84.603m cumulative deficit by 31 March 2026; £40.201m High Needs Block overspend
findings.quote: There is a forecast in-year deficit on the DSG in 2025-26 of £39.756m, which if added to the existing brought forward balance would result in a total cumulative deficit of £84.603m by 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Reserves depleted by £54.789m in 2022-23 and £58.763m in 2023-24, continuing downward trend with S151 warning
findings.detail: The council drew £54.789m reserves in 2022-23, £58.763m in 2023-24, and £3.032m in 2024-25. The S151 Officer's statement in February 2025 warned that 'further in-year budget overspends and failure to achieve the level of budget savings required would see the balance of the General Reserve substantially depleted and lead to issues around financial sustainability that would require urgent, radical savings'.
findings.matters: This is an unsustainable trajectory. The council's own finance officer has flagged that continued draws would trigger a solvency crisis. Lenders assess whether reserves can absorb shocks; a council burning £50m+ annually cannot.
findings.quote: This outturn positions for 2022-23 and 2023-24 resulted in the Council utilising reserves of £54.789m and £58.763m respectively, to balance the budget and meet inflationary and demand pressures.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care forecast overspend of £4.937m including £4.6m income shortfall from Community Charging
findings.detail: Community Charging income is £4.6m below budget. Care cost overruns of £2.1m in home care, £2.4m in residential and nursing, £1.1m in day care, and £1.3m in supported living reflect inflation, National Living Wage increases, and rising demand. The paper explicitly states these pressures are 'mainly unavoidable'.
findings.matters: A £4.6m income shortfall is a structural problem, not a demand spike. Unavoidable cost pressures from wage floors and inflation cannot be controlled or deferred.
findings.figures: £4.937m total overspend; £4.6m Community Charging income shortfall; home care £2.1m, residential/nursing £2.4m, day care £1.1m, supported living £1.3m
findings.quote: A shortfall in the level of income from Community Charging of £4.6m

findings.headline: Children's Services forecast overspend of £26.674m, primarily £15.7m on placements driven by high-cost residential provision
findings.detail: The overspend comprises £15.7m in placements (£11m agency residential, £4.9m in-house), £5.1m in education services driven by rising EHCP numbers, and £3.5m in home-to-school transport. The paper states this is due to lack of suitable foster care placements, complexity of need, and rising demand for SEND assessment and Educational Psychology services.
findings.matters: At £26.674m, this is an unbudgeted expenditure that persists despite 'substantial investment' made when the budget was set. It signals demand-driven cost pressures that budgeting cannot absorb.
findings.figures: £26.674m total overspend; £15.7m placements (£11m agency residential, £4.9m in-house); £5.1m education services; £3.5m home-to-school transport
findings.quote: A significant overspend in Placements of £15.7m. Overspend is primarily on agency residential placements (£11m) and in-house provision (£4.9m).

findings.headline: Reserve levels have reduced unsustainably and cannot continue funding pressures
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states that reserve levels "have reduced in recent years, as a result of both planned and unplanned use of reserves" and that this "is not sustainable and must be limited to one-off investments." Reserves have been drawn in 2022-23, 2023-24, and modestly in 2024-25, with further draws forecast for 2025-26.
findings.matters: A council cannot repeatedly fund operating pressures from reserves without creating a terminal sustainability crisis; this signals underlying structural deficit that must be closed through spending reductions or revenue sources.
findings.figures: Significant calls on reserves in 2022-23 and 2023-24; £3.082m use in 2024-25; £1.612m forecast draw in 2025-26
findings.quote: Historically the Council held a level of general fund and earmarked reserves that allowed some financial flexibility and the ability to invest in priority areas. However, levels have reduced in recent years, as a result of both planned and unplanned use of reserves to address significant revenue budget pressures. This is not sustainable and must be limited to one-off investments or to support the delivery of improvements and efficiencies.

findings.headline: Children's Services continues growing demand with high-cost residential placements
findings.detail: Children's Services faces £41.079m of cost and demand pressures in 2026-27, driven by growing numbers of children in care, increased complexity of need, and continued reliance on high-cost residential placements due to lack of internal and external foster care options. SEND-related costs (assessments, psychology, home-to-school transport) are also rising rapidly.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends that cannot easily be reversed signal structural service cost escalation that will affect future years regardless of savings efforts.
findings.figures: £41.079m Children's Services pressures 2026-27; forecast overspend £26.674m Q3 2025-26; numbers of children in care remain high with increasing complexity
findings.quote: Numbers of children in care remain high and with increasing complexity of need. This, coupled with a lack of suitable foster care placements internally and externally, is requiring continued use of high-cost residential placements, resulting in significant additional expenditure in excess of budget provision.

findings.headline: Escalating budget gap projected over medium term: £155m cumulative 2027-31
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan forecasts a cumulative budget gap of £155.009m over four years: £1.589m (2027-28), £33.453m (2028-29), £51.421m (2029-30), £68.695m (2030-31). This assumes all current savings plans are delivered and no further deterioration in demand pressures.
findings.matters: A structural budget deficit of this scale indicates the council faces either sustained savings delivery at scale or further reserve depletion and service reductions beyond the current plan.
findings.quote: This is an estimated total additional savings target of £155.009m over the four-year period 2027 to 2031 and assumes that all planned savings approved in 2025-26 and 2026-27 are delivered. Any significant changes to forecast future pressures or funding may increase or reduce this forecast future savings requirement.

findings.headline: 2026-27 budget depends entirely on delivery of £71.328m new savings programme
findings.detail: The council is balancing its 2026-27 budget through £71.328m of new savings (£63.895m ongoing, £7.433m one-off). The S151 Officer explicitly states that financial sustainability depends on delivery of these savings and that failure to deliver would prevent maintaining a balanced budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess delivery risk on savings of this magnitude against a backdrop of growing unfunded demand pressures in social care and prior difficulty containing overspends.
findings.figures: £71.328m new savings required for 2026-27; £63.895m ongoing, £7.433m one-off; additional £155.009m cumulative gap forecast 2027-28 to 2030-31
findings.quote: the Council's financial sustainability depends upon the proposed savings and efficiencies (Appendix 7) for 2026-27 being delivered. The Council must remain focussed on delivering savings as pressures have already been identified in future years as services expect many of the existing demand and cost pressures to continue.

findings.headline: 2025-26 forecast overspend of £1.612m forecast to trigger further reserve draw
findings.detail: Quarter 3 monitoring forecasts a £1.612m overspend for the current year, concentrated in Children's Services (£26.674m) and Adult Social Care (£4.937m). This will require drawing on reserves, following significant calls in 2022-23 and 2023-24.
findings.matters: Repeated in-year overspends and reserve depletion signal underlying pressure that budget controls are not containing spend, a concern for financial sustainability and lender confidence.
findings.figures: £1.612m forecast overspend Q3 2025-26; Children's £26.674m, Adult Care £4.937m; reserves called in 2022-23, 2023-24, and modestly in 2024-25 (£3.082m)
findings.quote: The Council's financial position remains challenging, with the continuing demand pressures and cost pressures in Children's Social Care and to a lesser extent in Adult Social Care. The Quarter 3 revenue monitoring forecast year-end position is for there to be an overspend of £1.612m.

findings.headline: £84m of unfunded SEND expenditure carried forward under statutory override
findings.detail: By March 2026, Derbyshire will hold approximately £84m of accumulated deficit from unfunded Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) services. The council's ability to present a balanced budget is currently dependent on the Statutory Override allowing these deficits to be excluded from the balance sheet.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that £84m of liabilities are being deferred via statutory mechanism rather than funded, representing a material contingent obligation if the override ends or requirements change.
findings.figures: £84m additional debt by March 2026; number of Education Health Care Plans (EHCPs) continues to grow
findings.quote: By March 2026, Derbyshire County Council is forecast to hold approximately £84m of additional debt arising from unfunded expenditure on statutory Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) services over several years. This represents one of the most significant financial risks for the Council with the ability to present a balanced budget currently being dependent on the Statutory Override allowing SEND deficits to be excluded from the Council's balance sheet.

findings.headline: Children's Services carrying persistent Red (20) rated financial overspend risk outside of DSG and placement costs
findings.detail: Beyond the tracked SEND and placement sufficiency deficits, Children's Services maintains a Red (20) financial pressure risk for other overspends, rated at the highest severity for loss (Band 8, over £20m). This has remained Red since at least December 2024 with no improvement trend visible.
findings.matters: Red rating indicates an unmanaged, escalating financial pressure across the whole directorate; no risk mitigation appears to be bringing it back to control
findings.figures: Red (20) rating across four quarters (Dec 2024 through Q2 2025-26); Band 8 financial impact (over £20m)
findings.quote: Children's Services financial pressures (non DSG) leading to overspend

findings.headline: National SEN deficit of £4.6bn creates two-year risk of Section 114 notices for two-fifths of local authorities
findings.detail: The National Audit Office reported in October 2024 that national SEN spending rose 58% over ten years without improving outcomes. A £4.6bn national deficit is driving two-fifths of councils toward insolvency notices when the statutory accounting override ends in March 2026. Derbyshire's Dedicated Schools Grant risk is rated Band 8 (over £20m).
findings.matters: Section 114 notice is statutory declaration of unbalanced budget triggering government intervention; two-year deadline for systemic resolution
findings.figures: £4.6bn national SEN deficit; 58% spending increase over 10 years; two-fifths of LAs at risk of Section 114 notice by March 2026; DSG risk Band 8 (over £20m)
findings.quote: There is a national financial deficit estimated at £4.6bn contributing in part to the risk of two-fifths of local authorities issuing a Section 114 notice by March 2026 when the accounting statutory override ends.

findings.headline: SEND budget deficit exceeds £6 million and continues to grow
findings.detail: Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) have exploded from 3,666 in 2019 to 7,164 in 2024, creating an unbudgeted £6m+ shortfall for assessments and home-to-school transport. Only 48% of assessments are completed within the statutory 20-week timeline.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted pressure on a statutory service growing faster than council can resource; directly impacts council's ability to deliver special needs provision
findings.figures: £6m+ deficit (June 2024); EHCPs increased from 3,666 (2019) to 7,164 (2024); 48% meeting 20-week assessment target
findings.quote: The council's budget deficit for EHCPs and home to school transport is over £6m (June 2024). Demand for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) increased from 3666 in 2019 to 7164 in 2024 (July 2024).

news_drafts.headline: £45m commercial property investment holding has £4.5m unrealised loss with expiring protection
news_drafts.lead: Crystallisation of the £4.5m loss would directly deplete reserves and require additional borrowing to offset, further reducing financial flexibility

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme forecast to require £55m+ in additional borrowing over next two years
news_drafts.lead: Rising debt levels increase future revenue commitments for debt service; particularly concerning as PWLB borrowing rates have risen significantly (10-year rate 5.38% → 5.72% during the year), making new borrowing more expensive

news_drafts.headline: Council deployed reserves to cover schools funding deficit, reducing financial buffers
news_drafts.lead: Declining reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or fund capital needs without additional borrowing, and may signal underlying service funding pressures
